clue.text: In the main a shocking character?

definitions.text: In the main a shocking character?

parts.words: In the main a shocking character?
parts.note: surface reading: someone appalling found in the main part of a group or story
setter's reading: 'the main' is the sea, and the creature lives in water and delivers an electric shock

explanation.surface: Someone scandalous lurking at the heart of things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The main' is an old poetic word for the open sea, and 'shocking' is literal: this fish stuns prey with electricity.
explanation.definitionFit: This South American fish can discharge hundreds of volts, so it is literally a shocking creature living in water.

clue.text: They may be exchanged after a proposal is accepted

definitions.text: They may be exchanged after a proposal is accepted

parts.words: They may be exchanged after a proposal is accepted
parts.note: surface reading: documents or contracts swapped once a business offer is agreed
setter's reading: the proposal is of marriage, after which a couple may swap tokens of betrothal

explanation.surface: Paperwork changing hands once a business deal is agreed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Proposal' and 'exchanged' sound like commerce, but the proposal here is of marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: After someone says yes to marrying, the couple wear bands marking their betrothal, sometimes giving one to each other.

clue.text: Call up second person sure to interrupt

indicators.note: something that interrupts breaks into the middle of another thing, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: in Genesis Eve was the second human created, after Adam
sure, as in 'all right', is OK

explanation.surface: Phoning someone while a confident second party butts in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second person' suggests grammar (you), but it means the second person in the Bible; OK goes inside to give EVOKE.
explanation.definitionFit: To call up a memory or feeling is to bring it to mind, which is exactly what this verb means.

clue.text: Having left will, Parisian is buried in famous gallery

indicators.note: something buried lies inside something else, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: the Tate is the well-known London art gallery
est is French for 'is', as a Parisian would say it

explanation.surface: A Frenchman's will found tucked away in a celebrated art gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is a group of British national art galleries; the French word goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal term for someone who died having made a valid will, the opposite of intestate.

clue.text: Vet in plain spectacles

indicators.note: the answer is found inside the run of words that follows, spanning them

parts.note: the letters run across the end of plain and the start of spectacles

explanation.surface: An animal doctor wearing ordinary glasses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vet' looks like the animal doctor, but here it is the verb meaning to check.
explanation.definitionFit: To vet something is to examine it carefully before approving it, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: The plane turned out to be a jumbo

indicators.note: turned out suggests the letters have been turned over and come out in a new order

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: The aircraft proved to be a jumbo jet.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'jumbo' as a jumbo jet, which suits a plane; here it is the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Jumbo is a familiar nickname for the large grey African or Asian beast, after the famous London Zoo animal.

clue.text: Stoppage during thunderstorm?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a sudden walkout by workers called without warning
second meaning: a bolt from the sky hitting something in a storm

explanation.walkthrough: A lightning strike in British usage is a sudden industrial action called with no notice; the question mark flags the literal second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names both a surprise work stoppage and an electrical discharge hitting the ground in a storm.

clue.text: Withdraw charter consumers introduced

indicators.note: something introduced is brought into another, so one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: to charter a boat or plane is to hire or rent it
CA is the Consumers' Association, the British consumer-rights body

explanation.surface: Pulling out of a charter deal once customers are brought in.
explanation.walkthrough: The Consumers' Association is the UK body behind the Which? magazine, abbreviated CA.
explanation.definitionFit: To recant is to take back a statement or belief formally, just as one may withdraw a claim.

clue.text: Gets worried about returning party stuff oneself

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so the word is read backwards
about means surrounding, so one piece wraps around the other
worried suggests something shaken up or agitated, so the letters are disturbed

parts.note: the letters to rearrange
a do is an informal word for a party

explanation.surface: Someone anxious about a party coming back, so they overeat.
explanation.walkthrough: GETS is rearranged to STGE, then the reversed party goes inside it to give STODGE.
explanation.definitionFit: As a British informal verb, to stodge means to gorge or fill up on heavy food.

clue.text: Absorb unmarried men, repulsively fat!

indicators.note: unmarried tells us to remove the abbreviation used for married, taking it out of the next word

parts.note: taken as written, before the married abbreviation M is dropped
gross can mean disgustingly overweight

explanation.surface: An insulting outburst about overweight bachelors.
explanation.walkthrough: M is the standard abbreviation for married, so 'unmarried men' means men without its M.
explanation.definitionFit: To engross is to occupy someone's full attention, as an absorbing book does.

clue.text: Heartlessly sell a number by trickery

indicators.note: without its heart, the word loses its middle and keeps only its outside letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of sell
eight is a number

explanation.surface: A cynical salesman shifting goods by sleight of hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A number' could be any number; the crossing letters pin it down to eight.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleight means cunning dexterity or deception, as in sleight of hand used by a conjuror.

clue.text: Get garage to change total

indicators.note: to change means the letters are altered into a different arrangement

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Instruction to take a car to the garage for a change of oil, totalling the bill.
explanation.definitionFit: An aggregate is a whole formed by combining parts, a sum such as a two-leg sporting score.

clue.text: Loathed Lawrence; had to imprison him

indicators.note: to imprison is to hold within walls, so one piece is shut inside the other

parts.note: taken as written
T E Lawrence, Lawrence of Arabia, known by his initials

explanation.surface: Someone so despised Lawrence that they had him locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: Lawrence of Arabia was T. E. Lawrence, so his initials stand for him here.
explanation.definitionFit: To have hated someone is to have loathed them; both are past-tense verbs of intense dislike.

clue.text: Break in, thanks to yours truly

parts.note: ta is British informal for thank you
yours truly is a jokey way of referring to oneself

explanation.surface: A burglar breaking in and crediting himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Break in' suggests a burglary, but it means training a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: To break in a horse is to train it to accept a rider, which is to make it docile.

clue.text: Coming after nine, let in around about ten

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so these letters enclose the next piece
about can mean in a disordered way, so the letters are moved around

parts.note: the letters to rearrange
X is the Roman numeral for ten

explanation.surface: A latecomer admitted around ten, after the nine o'clock crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coming after' is the definition, not part of the sequence; NINE LET IN is rearranged around X.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is next in line will follow the current person, so the phrase describes what comes after.

clue.text: One winning one with a queen

parts.note: a victor is the one who wins
I is the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A winner partnered by a queen, as in cards or chess.
explanation.walkthrough: The queen is Victoria, Britain's monarch from 1837 to 1901.
explanation.definitionFit: Victoria reigned over the United Kingdom for most of the nineteenth century, so she is an example of a queen.

clue.text: Container for drawers

parts.note: surface reading: a chest or cabinet that holds drawers, or a bag for underpants
setter's reading: drawers are people who draw, and their tools go in a small school pouch

explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawers' suggests furniture or knickers, but it means those who draw.
explanation.definitionFit: A small zipped pouch or box that holds pens and crayons for artists and schoolchildren.

clue.text: Exhibitionist very big in Peru, perhaps

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other
perhaps hints that the word is only a possible version, so its letters may be rearranged

parts.note: the letters to rearrange
OS is outsize, the clothing label for very big

explanation.surface: A show-off with a huge presence in Peru.
explanation.walkthrough: OS stands for outsize, a British clothing size; PERU is rearranged as PEUR around it.
explanation.definitionFit: A poseur behaves affectedly to impress others, which is what an exhibitionist does.

clue.text: Keep secret fuel NEC ordered inside

indicators.note: inside places one piece within the other

parts.note: coal is a fuel

indicators.note: ordered means arranged, so the three letters are put into a new sequence

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Hushing up an order of fuel placed with the NEC, Birmingham's exhibition centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fuel' wants to be a verb in the surface; it is the noun naming the fossil fuel.
explanation.definitionFit: To conceal something is to hide it from others, which means keeping it secret.

clue.text: Ray is spotted, if standing with mum

parts.note: saw is the past tense of see, meaning spotted

indicators.note: in a down clue standing means reading upward, so the short word is turned backwards

parts.note: taken as written
mum means silent, and sh is the call for silence

explanation.surface: Someone called Ray noticed standing alongside his mother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ray' looks like a man's name and 'mum' like a mother; ray is the fish and mum means keep quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: This long-snouted fish with a toothed blade is related to rays, a flat-bodied cartilaginous group.

clue.text: Eager to be a good shot, admittedly

parts.note: taken as written
to have a shot is to have a go
G is the standard abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Keen to be a decent marksman, one concedes.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces are taken in the order a, shot, good; 'admittedly' only rounds off the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone agog is full of eager curiosity, impatient to see or hear more.

clue.text: George wants to stop topless musical

indicators.note: in a down clue the top is the first letter, so topless means that letter is removed

parts.note: GR stands for Georgius Rex, King George
to cease is to stop

explanation.surface: George is keen to shut down a racy, bare-chested stage show.
explanation.walkthrough: GR is the royal cipher of a King George, seen on old British postboxes.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1971 stage show set in a 1950s high school, later a film with John Travolta, is a musical.

clue.text: Way to track peacock

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way
a rut is a groove or track worn in the ground

explanation.surface: Directions for following a strutting bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peacock' looks like the bird, but it is the verb meaning to show off.
explanation.definitionFit: To peacock is to parade oneself vainly, which is to swagger about proudly.

clue.text: Place inexperienced man on board

parts.note: someone inexperienced is new to the job
a castle, or rook, is a chess piece, a man on the chessboard

explanation.surface: Putting a novice on the company's board of directors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Place' looks like a verb, but it is the noun: Newcastle is a city in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Newcastle upon Tyne is a city, so it is an example of a place.

clue.text: Top admiral to execute sailors on deck

indicators.note: in a down clue the top of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of admiral
to execute a task is to do it
RN is the Royal Navy

explanation.surface: A senior admiral ordering sailors to be put to death on deck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deck' looks like a ship's deck, but it is the verb meaning to decorate.
explanation.definitionFit: To deck a hall with holly is to decorate it, and adorn is a synonym for that verb.

clue.text: Demoralise nun, ever misbehaving

indicators.note: misbehaving means acting out of order, so these letters fall into a new arrangement

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A nun who always behaves badly saps everyone's morale.
explanation.definitionFit: To unnerve someone is to make them lose courage or confidence, which is to dishearten them.

clue.text: The teeth of four Conservatives, when short of time!

indicators.note: short of means lacking, so the letter for time is taken away

parts.note: IV is the Roman numeral for four
Tories are members of Britain's Conservative Party

explanation.surface: Mocking the teeth of four Tory politicians who are pressed for time.
explanation.walkthrough: T is the standard abbreviation for time; the Tories are the UK Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivories is informal for teeth, from their white ivory colour, and also for piano keys.

clue.text: Pocket money?

parts.note: surface reading: the weekly allowance given to a child
setter's reading: the coins of low value that jingle in a trouser pocket

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase usually means a child's allowance, but here it is the loose coins that sit in a pocket.
explanation.definitionFit: Coins of low denomination are what people carry loose in their pockets, and the phrase also means a trivial sum.
